primitives.name: Spatial Density Ratio
primitives.verbatim_quote: This procedure allowed computing the number of attackers, defenders and ratio attackers/defenders on each of seven court locations (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 and A7) throughout the sequence of play, on a moment-to-moment basis.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'N_{\\text{attackers}}(t)': 'dimensionless count of attackers at time t', 'N_{\\text{defenders}}(t)': 'dimensionless count of defenders at time t', '\\rho_{\\text{ratio}}(t)': 'dimensionless ratio of attackers to defenders'}
primitives.assumptions: Players are modeled as point masses; court is partitioned into discrete zones with fixed boundaries.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When $ N_{\text{defenders}}(t) \to 0 $, $ \rho_{\text{ratio}}(t) \to \infty $, indicating potential for offensive breakthrough.

layer2.mapping: The ratio serves as a kernel for Bayesian inference in GSI to predict success probability of offensive plays.
layer2.telemetry: Momentary counts of attackers and defenders per zone.

primitives.name: Relative Position to Basket
primitives.verbatim_quote: We found that player's spatial distribution proceeds in function of the relative position to the basket.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'d_{\\text{rel}}(p_i, \\text{basket})': 'meters distance from player $ p_i $ to basket', '\\vec{p}_i': 'position vector of player $ i $', '\\vec{b}': 'position vector of basket'}
primitives.assumptions: Basket is a fixed reference point; Euclidean distance is used for simplicity.
primitives.breakdown_regime: As $ d_{\text{rel}} \to 0 $, spatial density increases, leading to higher interaction frequency.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSE's state-space representation where proximity to basket triggers tactical adjustments.
layer2.telemetry: Real-world coordinates of players and basket via TACTO software.

primitives.name: Numerical Superiority Defensive
primitives.verbatim_quote: Particularly, defensive numerical superiority in closer areas to the basket (A3) was related with higher offensive efficacy.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\Delta N_{\\text{def}}(A3)': 'dimensionless difference in player counts in area A3', 'N_{\\text{defenders}}(A3)': 'count of defenders in area A3', 'N_{\\text{attackers}}(A3)': 'count of attackers in area A3'}
primitives.assumptions: Area A3 is defined as the painted area; numerical superiority implies defensive dominance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When $ \Delta N_{\text{def}}(A3) < 0 $, indicates vulnerability to offensive pressure.

layer2.mapping: Used in GSI to compute conditional probability of offensive success given defensive strength.
layer2.telemetry: Counts of players in A3 during key moments of play.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that collective spatial behavior in basketball is governed by momentary numerical imbalances between attackers and defenders within discrete court zones. The derived spatial density ratio provides a continuous measure of these imbalances, which can be interpreted as a stochastic process over time. This allows GSI to model offensive efficacy as a probabilistic outcome conditioned on the ratio of attackers to defenders in each zone. The relative position to the basket introduces a spatial bias, where proximity to the basket correlates with increased interaction density and thus affects the likelihood of successful plays. Numerical superiority in close proximity to the basket (specifically A3) acts as a stabilizing factor, increasing the probability of offensive success. These primitives form a dual framework: one for static spatial configuration and another for dynamic interaction dynamics. The failure mode occurs when spatial density is misinterpreted due to insufficient temporal resolution or inaccurate player tracking data. The mathematical structure supports both Bayesian inference and Markovian state transitions in GSE.
